title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days before the CIA Challenge Exam, after you have worked through the notes and taken your mocks. Nothing in it is new. Most days take about an hour; the two mock days and the day after the full mock take longer.
how_it_works: No new topics this week. Late new material crowds out what you have already learned.
One full timed mock at the real three-hour length early in the week, then no more full mocks. The last days are for recall and rest.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Time follows the exam weights: Section D, the largest at 25%, comes first; Sections A, C and E, 20% each, get a day each; Section B, 15%, shares one.
The Challenge turns on your seat and three close pairs: approve or tell, must or should, function or engagement. A few minutes a day keeps them apart.
Coming from CISA? Some tasks also name a lesson from the Coming from CISA notes. Candidates on other pathways can skip those lines.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan. Missed a day? Skip it and carry on; never double up.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the real length, ideally at your exam's start time, to rehearse pace and three hours of focus.

tasks.text: Warm up for five minutes: name your seat for three topics, the charter, an engagement's work program and risk that management accepts. Then check the principle.
Take a full timed mock in one sitting: 150 questions in 180 minutes, phone away, no notes.
Pace by two checkpoints: question 75 by minute 90; question 125 by minute 150. Stuck on one? Choose your best answer, flag it and move on.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: A mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. KaiSip shows percent by section; that is not The IIA's scaled score and cannot predict your result.

days.title: Learn from your misses
days.goal: Trace each mock miss to its thinking slip, then recall Section D, the largest at 25%. Stop at about 90 minutes.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from the mock, newest first.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list five Section D points, from evidence to the conclusion. Then open the list and check.
Say the three tests for information, in order, and when evidence is enough. Then check the principles on proving it. From CISA? Also read lesson 4X5.1.

days.remember: Evidence is enough when another competent person could repeat the work and agree, not when you feel sure.

days.title: The three close pairs
days.goal: Drill the pairs the Challenge turns on, recall Section A, and work on the section furthest behind its weight.

tasks.text: Approve or tell: name what the board approves, and what is only reported in time, such as plan gaps and a money shortfall. Then check the note.
Must or should: say the three steps for accepted risk with the strength of each, and why the should step still comes FIRST. Then check the principles on reading.
Function or engagement: name two decisions that are the chief audit executive's for the function, and two that belong to one engagement. Then check the principles on your seat.
From memory, list five Section A points: mandate, independence, objectivity, confidentiality and quality. Then open the list and check. From CISA? Also read lesson 4X1.2.
Answer a short untimed set in your focus section. Before each answer, name the seat and whether the question asks for a must or a should.

days.remember: The board approves only where a Standard says so. Asked what is required, a should loses; asked what comes FIRST, it can win.

days.title: Pace check and planning
days.goal: Keep your pace sharp with one short timed mock, then recall Section C in engagement order and the rules that keep auditors objective.

tasks.text: Take the short timed mock in one sitting. Watch your pace more than the score.
From memory, list five Section C points in engagement order, from objectives to resources. Then open the list and check.
Say where criteria come from first, what the work program holds and when it is approved. Then check the note. From CISA? Also read lesson 4X4.2.
Say why fraud risk enters every engagement risk assessment, and name the three sides of the fraud triangle. Then check the principles on what drives the work.
Say why an internal auditor may not give assurance on an area they ran last year, and who hears about it. Then check the principles on staying unbiased.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Results and the plan
days.goal: Recall Sections E and B from the chief audit executive's seat, redo your mistakes, and work on your second gap.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Section E points and three Section B points, and say who approves or is told in each. Then open the lists and check.
Say the steps after an action's date is missed, in order, and who judges what the delay means. Then check the note. From CISA? Also read lesson 4X6.5.
Say how a finding fixed before issue is reported, and what happens to a significant error found after issue. Then check the principles on speaking up.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.
Practice a short untimed set in your second-weakest section. Find the priority word before you read the options.

days.remember: Management owns the action and internal audit confirms it. A request is an input, not an order, and reliance follows evaluation.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Touch everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each section, recall two points before you open its list, starting with Section D. If one will not come back, open its note for that point only.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Say the three pairs once more: approve or tell, must or should, function or engagement. Then glance at the one-line rules.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your appointment, the test center's address and your route. Read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's candidate handbook.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: say the answering steps and your two checkpoints from memory, then check them. Stop after 15 minutes.
Read the one-line rule for your most common slip on the principles list.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your appointment is confirmed, and you have read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's current candidate handbook.
Your route to the test center and your travel time are planned, with a backup.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine. Three hours is long, so start the day fed.
Reread your two checkpoints: question 75 by minute 90; question 125 by minute 150.
Leave early enough that a delay on the way would not matter.
Your seat moves with the topic: an internal auditor who knows the rules, the internal auditor running an engagement, or the chief audit executive. Management owns the fix.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and move on.

points.text: The board grants the mandate and approves the charter; senior management gives input and support. The chief audit executive supplies the information, drafts the charter and discusses it with both.

Independence belongs to the function. The chief audit executive confirms it to the board at least yearly, including any impairment and its safeguards, and discusses roles that may impair it with the board and senior management.

Three Lines Model: management owns and manages risk, second-line roles support and monitor it, and internal audit gives independent assurance and advice. Internal audit may advise and challenge, never decide or own a risk response.
Objectivity is each auditor's mind. No assurance on an activity you were responsible for within the past 12 months; disclose an impairment first, and let the right party decide the safeguard.
Information from the work is for the work: share it only with authorized people or under a legal or professional duty. Confidentiality never keeps a finding from the board.

An external assessment is due at least once every 5 years, by a qualified, independent assessor or team with at least one active CIA. The board approves the plan and receives the complete results directly.

Match a nonconformance disclosure to its reach: one engagement in its final communication, the whole function to the board and senior management, with its impact. Claim conformance only where support exists.

domains.name: Internal Audit Operations and Audit Plan

points.text: Outsource the work, never the responsibility. Contracted auditors follow the Standards, the chief audit executive supervises their engagements, and the board still approves an adequate budget.
Build the budget from the strategy and plan, and seek the board's approval. When money falls short, promptly report the impact to the board and senior management; never trim the plan quietly.

The strategy holds a vision, strategic objectives and initiatives, reviewed periodically with the board and senior management. No Standard asks the board to approve it; the plan is what the board approves.
Report formally, relate informally. Give the board what it needs for oversight, not only what it asks for. Meeting the board privately at least once a year is a should.
A request is an input, not an order. Weigh it against risk and resources, and report conflicting demands between major stakeholders to the board and senior management.

The plan rests on a documented risk assessment, done at least yearly. The board approves the plan and its significant changes; an urgent change is told to the board at once and approved formally soon after.
Rely on another provider's work only after evaluating it, and document the basis. When coordination fails, go to senior management first and the board if necessary.

Objectives come from the activity's strategy, risks and processes; the scope must cover every objective. When assurance covers a Topical Requirement's topic, assess each requirement and record why any is excluded.
Change objectives or scope only with approval, then tell management in time. A change of dates alone, with nothing else changed, needs no approval: tell management promptly.
Criteria start from what the board and senior management have set, if adequate. If not, work out better ones with them. Settle criteria before testing; advisory work may need none.
Build the engagement's own ranked list of significant risks, fraud included, at planning. Rank by impact and likelihood against the organization's thresholds, never by how easy a risk is to test.

Fraud basics: fraud needs intent, error does not. Know the triangle of pressure, opportunity and rationalization; controls reach opportunity. Classify a scheme by the act: false reporting, misused assets or corruption.
No fieldwork before the work program is approved: criteria, tasks, methods, tools and an assigned auditor for each objective, with every later change approved promptly.

Short of resources? Raise it with the chief audit executive; never trim quietly. A cut needs approval and must still reach every objective, and a constraint that stops planned work is a scope limitation.
Information must be relevant, reliable and sufficient: enough that an informed, competent person could repeat the work and agree. More volume never repairs irrelevant or unreliable evidence.
Evidence the auditor obtains directly outweighs what the activity hands over; corroboration and a well-controlled source add weight. An interview alone rarely proves that a control operates.
Expectation first, then comparison, then follow-up. A ratio, variance or analytics flag shows where to look; it becomes a potential finding only after follow-up shows a gap against criteria.

A finding is the condition measured against the criteria. Ask why until you reach the root cause, find it with management where possible, and weigh significance by likelihood and impact, not money alone.
Workpapers pass when a competent stranger could repeat the work and reach the same result. Every result traces back to its finding, its test and its evidence.
A conclusion weighs the findings together; it does not count them. For assurance, say how effective governance, risk management and control are, including when they work.

Supervise from planning to sign-off. Before results go out, the supervisor checks that the workpapers support them and asks for evidence rather than rewriting a conclusion. Urgent issues are raised during the work.

Every final communication: objectives, scope, conclusions, recommendations or action plans, owners and dates. Assurance adds findings with significance and priority, scope limitations and a conclusion on effectiveness.
Management owns the action. A good plan reaches the root cause, has an owner and a date, and brings the risk within tolerance. Repairing the items found is only a start.

Internal auditors draft; the chief audit executive reviews and approves before issue and decides who receives it. A release outside the organization waits for any required legal or senior management advice.
A finding fixed before issue is reported with the action acknowledged, never deleted. A significant error is corrected promptly for everyone who received the original.

Accepted risk above appetite or tolerance: the responsible management first (a should), then senior management (a must), then the board if unresolved (a must). The chief audit executive never resolves it.
Follow up by inquiry, risk-based assessment and tracking, scaled to significance. Past due shows as past due, and nothing closes until internal audit confirms it.

A missed date: document management's explanation and take it to the chief audit executive, who judges whether the delay means risk beyond tolerance was accepted. If so, the accepted-risk route follows.

principles.intro: The mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. In an engagement, understand the activity and its risks before setting objectives, and approve the work program before testing. For accepted risk, the responsible management comes before senior management and the board.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which step does this one depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the one that keeps you in the seat the topic gives you, with approval left to the board or the supervisor and action left to management.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one keeps me in my seat?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST reliable evidence or MOST important matter to report to the board. Judge the options on that quality only.
The main purpose or reason, not a side benefit. Follow-up exists to confirm that management acted; a quality program exists to show conformance and drive improvement.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For a finding or an accepted risk, weigh likelihood and impact against the organization's appetite or tolerance, not the money alone.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and against which limit?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What the facts given most probably point to, such as what an unexpected variance or a pattern of missed action dates means, even if another outcome would be worse.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what usually follows from these facts?

priority_words.meaning: Flip the test. Three options fit, and you want the one that helps or fits least. Slow down when you see it.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is asked: an action, a person, a document, a test or a reason.

answering_routine.title: Name the seat from the topic
answering_routine.text: Mandate, independence or objectivity: an internal auditor who knows the rules. One engagement: the internal auditor doing it. The whole function: the chief audit executive. An option from another seat is often the trap.

answering_routine.title: Find the actor and the priority word
answering_routine.text: Internal auditor, supervisor, chief audit executive, the board, senior management or the management responsible? Then spot FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options where internal audit decides for management, approval is sought where no Standard requires it, a step in the order or the route is skipped, or a should is called a must.

answering_routine.title: Settle the final two with a principle
answering_routine.text: Ask who approves, who must be told and when, and who owns the action. Say the reason in one sentence, then answer.

pace: 150 questions in 180 minutes is 1.2 minutes each. Use that to set checkpoints, not to time each question.
Checkpoints: question 75 by minute 90; question 125 by minute 150. Look at the clock there and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? Those minutes are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few; do not rush them all.
Stuck? Choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so never leave a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one. Three hours is long: settle in for one sitting.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as a seat, an actor, a must or should, or a priority word you missed the first time.
